title: All things new (Revelation 21:5–8)
hook: behold, I make all things new

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new heaven and a new earth: God dwelling with people, and no more death, mourning or crying. Your line was no more tears. Who did you stay with a little while? Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

A chipped bowl, glued back together, the crack still showing. A coat with a patch on the elbow. A friendship that broke and then, slowly, didn't. Mending doesn't swap one thing for another thing. It's the same thing, made whole. John has just seen a new heaven and a new earth, and a holy city coming down. Now the one sitting on the throne speaks, and the King James Bible gives the words like this: "Behold, I make all things new." Listen to the order. Not all new things. All things, new. Today we stay with that one sentence, and the lines that follow it.
screen: `NOT ALL NEW THINGS. ALL THINGS, NEW.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence itself: "And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new." Some readers lean on the wording. The old world isn't thrown out while a fresh one is unpacked; the things themselves are made new. Other readers hear a cleaner break, because verse one says the first heaven and the first earth "were passed away." Christians hold both readings, and the chapter holds both lines. Second, the tense. The King James says I make, not I will make. Some readers hear it already under way, not only at the end of the story. Paul writes something close in his second letter to Corinth: "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." Third, the next breath. John is told, "Write: for these words are true and faithful." Then: "It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end." The one who started the story is the one who finishes it. And a gift follows: "I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely." Freely. Thirst is the only thing the verse asks for. Fourth, the hard edge. Verse eight doesn't stop at comfort. It names the fearful, the unbelieving, murderers, liars and others, and gives them their part in the lake of fire. Christians read that verse in more than one way: as a real judgment, as a warning meant to turn people around, or as a picture of what can't live in a world made whole. The passage keeps the promise and the warning side by side.

Here's the practice: make one thing new. Not a renovation. One small thing within reach. A smudged glass. A crooked picture. A message you meant to answer that's gone stale on your phone. Choose it now, before the bell. Then settle, and breathe. For the length of the sit, hold that one thing in your mind and see it made fresh: clean, straight, answered. Notice that it's still itself. If you pray, you can hold the words "Behold, I make all things new" in the quiet. If you don't, just breathe with the one thing you chose. The bell holds the time.
All things new. The promise from the throne in Revelation twenty-one, heard by some readers as the same things made whole, and by others as a fresh start after the old has passed away.
Your line: all things new. Today, make your one thing new with your own hands, and leave it where you'll see it again tonight. Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Some churches read Revelation 21 at funerals, and Christians also hear its 'all things new' alongside Paul's words about becoming a new creature in Christ.

original.note: Greek: new I make all things. in Revelation 21:5 the word for new comes first.

trapdoor: what you thought: God throws the old world away and starts from scratch.
what it means: the one on the throne says "I make all things new"; some readers hear the things themselves made whole, others a clean new start.
what a scholar hears: kaina poio panta, in the present tense, with new placed first; readers weigh it beside verse 1, where the first heaven and earth pass away.
